nameStory: The "leatherleaf" name comes from the plant's distinctive evergreen leaves that feel thick and tough like leather when you touch them. These sturdy leaves have a wrinkled, textured surface that really does remind you of old leather that's been creased and worn over time.
description: Leatherleaf viburnum is a robust evergreen shrub that stands out in the landscape with its coarse, textured appearance. It grows into a large, upright shrub reaching 10-15 feet tall and wide, making it quite substantial in the garden. The plant is covered in long, oval leaves that are dark blue-green on top and pale green underneath, giving it a distinctive two-toned look. In spring, it produces clusters of creamy-white fragrant flowers, followed by berries that start blue and ripen to glossy black.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long oval leaves up to 8 inches that feel thick and leathery to the touch, with deeply impressed veins creating a wrinkled, textured surface. Dark blue-green on top, pale green underneath.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Large evergreen shrub growing 10-15 feet tall and wide with an upright, coarse appearance that stays green year-round.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Fragrant creamy-white flowers bloom in flat-topped clusters in spring, creating a showy display against the dark foliage.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Berries start blue in early summer, becoming plump and glossy black by fall, often persisting into winter.

idTips.label: Leaf Stems
idTips.description: Fuzzy brown leaf stems (petioles) that feel soft and velvety when rubbed between your fingers.

habitat: As a non-native Asian species, leatherleaf viburnum is primarily found in cultivated settings like parks, gardens, and landscaped areas throughout New England. It's occasionally found naturalized near old homesites or where garden waste has been dumped. The plant tolerates various soil conditions but prefers well-drained sites in partial shade to full sun.

seasonality.spring: Fragrant creamy-white flower clusters bloom, filling the air with sweet perfume. New growth emerges on branch tips.
seasonality.summer: Blue berries form and begin to ripen. The thick evergreen leaves provide consistent identification through hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Berries mature to glossy black and become quite showy against the dark foliage. Leaves remain green and leathery.
seasonality.winter: Evergreen leaves persist, often looking somewhat droopy in cold weather. Black berries may remain on branches, providing winter interest.

funFact: The deeply wrinkled leaf surface isn't just for show - those impressed veins and thick, leathery texture help the plant survive harsh winters by reducing water loss and protecting against cold damage, which is why it can stay evergreen even in New England's frigid climate.
confusionNotes: The evergreen nature and large size set it apart from most other viburnums in New England, which are deciduous. The thick, wrinkled leaves are unlike any native viburnum - if the leaves feel leathery and stay green in winter, you've found leatherleaf viburnum.
contextualKnowledge: This Asian native was introduced as an ornamental plant and is still popular in landscaping for its evergreen nature and showy berries. However, it's extremely rare in the wild in New England - there's only been one recorded observation, suggesting it doesn't naturalize well in our climate despite being hardy enough for cultivation.
compareHints: Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round. Its leaves are much larger, thicker, and more textured than species like hobblebush or arrowwood viburnums. The fuzzy brown leaf stems are also unique among the viburnum family in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
